title: The Spice Islands
blurb: Cloves and nutmeg once sent ships across oceans and started wars. How did tiny islands in Indonesia change the world?

chapters.title: The Smell of Fortune
chapters.text:
Open a kitchen cupboard and you may find small jars of cinnamon, pepper, cloves and nutmeg. We sprinkle them on food without thinking much about them. Yet for hundreds of years, these spices were among the most valuable goods in the world. Ships crossed oceans for them, and wars were fought over them.

A spice is a part of a plant, such as a seed, a piece of bark, a bud or a root, that we use to give flavour or fragrance. Cinnamon is the bark of a tree. A peppercorn is a dried berry.

People wanted spices for many reasons. They gave food a rich taste and filled a room with sweet smells, and some were used as medicine. In Europe, wealthy families served spiced food at feasts to show how rich they were. In China long ago, officials at the emperor's court held cloves in their mouths to sweeten their breath before they spoke to him.

You may have heard that people used spices to hide the taste of bad meat. Many historians doubt this. Spices often cost far more than meat, so anyone who could afford them could also afford fresh food.

Many spices come from the warm, wet lands near the equator. This is why the story of spices is so closely tied to the islands of Southeast Asia. There, the sun is strong and the rain falls almost every month. A clove tree would never survive a cold European winter. So people in the cold north could not simply grow their own. They had to buy spices from far away, at a very high price.

That is where this story begins, with a small, sweet-smelling bud on a faraway island and with people on the other side of the world who would do almost anything to get it.

chapters.title: Islands of Spice
chapters.text:
Two of the most precious spices came from a handful of small islands in eastern Indonesia, in the part of the country now called Maluku. Old maps call them the Spice Islands.

Cloves grew naturally on a few islands in the north of Maluku, such as Ternate and Tidore. These two islands are really the tops of volcanoes rising out of the sea, and clove trees love the rich soil and the humid air. A clove is the dried flower bud of the tree, and it is picked before it opens. Pickers spread the buds on mats in the sun until they turn dark brown. The English name comes from an old French word for a nail, because a dried clove looks like a tiny nail.

Nutmeg grew on the Banda Islands, a tiny group far to the south of Ternate and Tidore, in the deep Banda Sea. The nutmeg tree gives two spices. Its fruit looks a little like a small peach, and it splits open when it is ripe. The seed inside the fruit is nutmeg, and the red net that wraps around the seed is called mace.

For a long time, these trees did not grow in any other place on Earth. This made the spices rare, and rare things are expensive. Most buyers in Europe had no idea where the spices came from, and the traders had good reason not to tell them.

The people of these islands looked after the trees for generations. The sultans of Ternate and Tidore grew rich and powerful from the clove trade, and the two islands were great rivals. The Banda Islands were too small to grow much rice, so Bandanese merchants traded their nutmeg for rice and cloth from other islands. They were skilled traders, and they knew exactly what their spice was worth.

questions.why: The traders earned money by standing between the islands and the buyers. A buyer who knew the source would no longer need them.

chapters.title: Along the Sea Roads
chapters.text:
The spices did not stay on the islands. Local traders carried them in their boats to ports on Java, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula. From there, merchants from India, Arabia and China bought them and shipped them west and north. Melaka, on the Malay Peninsula, became one of the greatest of these ports. One Portuguese visitor wrote that eighty-four languages could be heard in its streets.

These voyages depended on the monsoon, a seasonal wind that changes direction during the year. For about half the year, the wind blows from one side. Then it turns and blows from the opposite side. Sailors learned to sail out with one wind and come home with the other. A ship that missed the turn of the wind might wait in port for months.

So the ports filled with sailors who were waiting, trading and learning each other's words. Many of them used Malay as a shared language of trade. Much later, that language grew into Bahasa Indonesia.

Goods were only part of what travelled along these sea roads. New words, new foods and new beliefs came too. Islam, for example, reached many island ports with Muslim traders and teachers, and it became the faith of many people there.

By the time the spices reached Europe, they had passed through many hands. Ships took them across the Indian Ocean, and camels and boats carried them on to ports such as Alexandria in Egypt. There, merchants from Venice bought them and sold them across Europe. Each trader added a little to the price. A pinch of pepper in a London kitchen cost many times more than it did at the port where it was loaded.

Rulers in Europe looked at these prices and began to wonder if there was another way to reach the spices.

chapters.title: Ships from Far Away
chapters.text:
At the end of the 1400s, Portuguese sailors found a way around the south of Africa and into the Indian Ocean. In 1511, they captured Melaka. Then, in 1512, ships from Portugal reached the Banda Islands. The Portuguese wanted to buy spices directly, without the many traders in between. This was a big change, because European ships had never before come so far east, and the voyage from Portugal took many months.

Spain came too. In 1521, two ships from the expedition of Ferdinand Magellan reached Tidore and loaded cloves. Magellan himself had been killed on the way. Only one ship, the Victoria, reached Spain again, after sailing around the whole world. The cloves it carried were worth a fortune, enough to cover much of the cost of the voyage.

The islanders did not simply accept these newcomers. In 1575, the people of Ternate, led by Sultan Baabullah, drove the Portuguese out of their fort after a long siege.

In 1602, a group of Dutch merchants started a powerful company called the Dutch East India Company, known by its Dutch initials as the VOC. It had its own ships, its own soldiers and its own rules. It could even make treaties and fight wars.

The VOC wanted to control the whole spice trade. It forced the local people to sell only to the company, at low prices. The people of Banda had sold to whoever they liked for centuries, and many of them refused. In 1621, on the orders of its governor, the company's soldiers attacked the islands. Thousands of people were killed, enslaved or forced to flee. Some escaped by boat to the Kei Islands, where their descendants still speak the Banda language today.

Life on the islands changed for ever, and many people suffered because of this. Their story is an important part of Indonesian history.

chapters.title: A Tiny Island and a Big Deal
chapters.text:
In the 1600s, the Netherlands and England competed for the spice islands. One of the places they fought over was Run, a very small island in the Banda group. Run was only about three kilometres long, but it was covered in nutmeg trees. It was the last place in Banda where the English had a foothold. For nearly four years, a small group of English sailors held out there against the Dutch, until their captain, Nathaniel Courthope, was killed in 1620. The Dutch took control of Run, but England went on claiming it.

Now travel to the other side of the world. In North America, Dutch settlers had built a small trading town on an island called Manhattan, on land where the Lenape people had long lived. The Dutch called the town New Amsterdam. In 1664, English ships sailed in and took it without a fight, and they gave it a new name: New York.

So each country now held something the other one wanted. In 1667, the two countries signed an agreement called the Treaty of Breda. England gave up its claim to Run. In exchange, the Dutch gave up their claim to New Amsterdam. Today, New Amsterdam is known as New York City, and the part where the Dutch had settled is still called Manhattan. It is one of the busiest places in the world.

Back then, people thought the Dutch had made a good bargain. A tiny island with nutmeg trees seemed more valuable than a big piece of land. Nutmeg made fortunes, while New Amsterdam was a muddy little town of about fifteen hundred people.

Today, Run is still small and quiet, and Manhattan has more than a million and a half people. Nobody in 1667 could have guessed that. And nobody asked the people of Run, or the Lenape, what they wanted.

chapters.title: Spices Today
chapters.text:
The Dutch tried to keep the nutmeg and clove trees only on their own islands. The company's patrol boats cut down clove trees on other islands, and nutmeg seeds sold abroad were treated so that they could not grow. But it was not possible to guard every seed for ever. Even the birds were against them, because pigeons ate nutmeg fruit and dropped the seeds on other islands.

In the 1700s and 1800s, seedlings were taken to other warm places, such as Mauritius, the Caribbean and Zanzibar. In about 1770, a French official called Pierre Poivre had clove and nutmeg seedlings smuggled to Mauritius. His family name, Poivre, is the French word for pepper. Later, Zanzibar became famous for cloves. The Caribbean island of Grenada grew so much nutmeg that a small picture of a nutmeg appears on its flag today.

Once the trees grew elsewhere, spices became cheaper. The VOC, once so powerful, ran into huge debts and was closed down at the end of 1799.

Today, you can buy spices cheaply in any market. Indonesia is still one of the biggest producers of nutmeg and cloves in the world. In Indonesian kitchens, people use cloves, nutmeg and many other spices in dishes such as soto and rendang. Visitors can still walk through the nutmeg groves of Banda, under tall trees planted long ago to give them shade.

Clove oil is still used in some medicines for the teeth, too. The story of spices reminds us that things that seem small can have a big influence on history. It began with a tiny bud and a small island. It carried new languages and new beliefs across the sea, and it brought great suffering as well. So the next time you smell a bowl of soto, remember how far that smell has travelled.

questions.prompt: How did the VOC try to stop other places from growing nutmeg?
options: By giving away free nutmeg to people in other lands
By treating the seeds it sold so that they could not grow
By asking the birds to stay away from the fruit
By paying other countries to plant only coffee trees
questions.why: Nutmeg seeds sold abroad were treated so that they could not grow.

questions.prompt: How did pigeons work against the Dutch plan?
options: They carried messages to the other traders on other islands
They ate all of the young clove buds before they could open
They ate nutmeg fruit and dropped the seeds on other islands
They damaged the company's patrol boats with their droppings
questions.why: Pigeons ate nutmeg fruit and dropped the seeds on other islands.

questions.prompt: What did Pierre Poivre do?
options: He started the Dutch East India Company
He wrote a book about the pepper trade
He sailed all the way around the world
He had seedlings smuggled to Mauritius
questions.why: In about 1770, Pierre Poivre had clove and nutmeg seedlings smuggled to Mauritius.

questions.prompt: What does the picture on Grenada's flag tell us?
options: Nutmeg has been very important to that island
The people of Grenada do not grow nutmeg now
Grenada was the first home of the nutmeg tree
Grenada was once ruled by the Banda Islands
questions.why: The text says Grenada grew so much nutmeg that a small picture of a nutmeg appears on its flag. A flag shows what a country values.

questions.prompt: What happened to spice prices once the trees grew elsewhere?
options: They became cheaper
They became higher
They became a secret
They stayed the same
questions.why: Once the trees grew elsewhere, spices became cheaper.

questions.prompt: Why might the VOC have lost its power after other places began growing spices?
options: Its ships had all been sold to traders in Zanzibar
It no longer had control of something that was rare
Its leaders had decided to give the islands back
Its soldiers had all gone home to the Netherlands
questions.why: The company's power came from controlling rare spices. Once trees grew elsewhere, spices became cheaper, and the company ran into debt and was closed.

questions.prompt: Which country is still among the biggest producers of nutmeg and cloves?
options: Mauritius
England
Indonesia
The Netherlands
questions.why: Indonesia is still one of the biggest producers of nutmeg and cloves in the world.

questions.prompt: What is the main message of the book?
options: Spices have always been bad for people who eat too many
Only people from Europe have ever used spices in their food
The Spice Islands are no longer important to anyone at all
Small things such as spices can have a big influence on history
questions.why: The last chapter says things that seem small can have a big influence on history, and that it began with a tiny bud and a small island.
